comments.text:
Undervolting your GPU does nothing to resolve bottlenecks. In fact, it could make them worse depending on the GPU. 

The bottleneck described in this video is the most noticeable and least desirable one, a CPU bottleneck. Undervolting your GPU doesn't change it's performance much, if at all, on most modern hardware, in fact it may even make the GPU run faster. By pulling voltage your GPU will run cooler, but it can come at the cost of instability, most modern GPUs however have the ability to boost their clocks above their specified speeds so long as there's thermal and power headroom. Voltage reduces thermals *and* power consumption, meaning there's less heat and more power available for this boosting process.

A brief note on power headroom, voltage isn't power, more specifically power in this case is wattage. Computing silicon has a ton of different design specifications, one of which is how many watts it can take. For example my RX 6900 XT has a wattage rating around 300 watts depending on the AIB card, this is sometimes called "TGP," or total graphics power, not to be confused with "TDP," or thermal design power. Basically this means the silicon is designed to pull up to 300W under load.

By reducing the voltage the wattage needed by the GPU decreases and less heat is generated, meaning more thermal and headroom which boost clocks can take advantage of.

A really good example of this happening is AMD's 5000 series X3D CPUs which are known to have some thermal headroom issues due to its fundamental design. I actually undervolted my 5700X3D and saw a significant improvement in average core clocks *and* temperatures.
